questions.subject: physics
questions.question_text: If the earth were to suddenly contract to half of its present radius, what would be the duration of the day?
questions.question_html: If the earth were to suddenly contract to half of its present radius, what would be the duration of the day?
questions.explanation_text: When the earth contracts suddenly, no external torque is acting on it. So its angular momentum remains conserved. Angular momentum is $L=I\omega$ For a spherical body, $I∝R^{2}$ If the radius becomes half, $R^{'}=\frac{R}{2}$ So the new moment of inertia becomes $I^{'}=I(\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{I}{4}$ Using conservation of angular momentum, $I\omega=I^{'}\omega^{'}$ $I\omega=\frac{I}{4}\omega^{'}$ $\omega^{'}=4\omega$ So the earth will rotate $4$ times faster. Time period is inversely proportional to angular velocity, so $T^{'}=\frac{T}{4}$ Present duration of a day is $T=24\text{h}$ Hence, $T^{'}=\frac{24}{4}=6\text{h}$ So the duration of the day would be $6\text{h}$ Correct option: Option A.
questions.explanation_html:
When the earth contracts suddenly, no external torque is acting on it. So its angular momentum remains conserved.

Angular momentum is

$L=I\omega$

For a spherical body,

$I∝R^{2}$

If the radius becomes half,

$R^{'}=\frac{R}{2}$

So the new moment of inertia becomes

$I^{'}=I(\frac{1}{2})^{2}=\frac{I}{4}$

Using conservation of angular momentum,

$I\omega=I^{'}\omega^{'}$

$I\omega=\frac{I}{4}\omega^{'}$

$\omega^{'}=4\omega$

So the earth will rotate $4$ times faster.

Time period is inversely proportional to angular velocity, so

$T^{'}=\frac{T}{4}$

Present duration of a day is

$T=24\text{h}$

Hence,

$T^{'}=\frac{24}{4}=6\text{h}$

So the duration of the day would be

$6\text{h}$

Correct option: Option A.

questions.explanation_text: The angular momentum of a moving body remains constant if net external torque is not applied . So the correct option is: Option D: net external torque is not applied According to the principle of conservation of angular momentum, if the net external torque acting on a body or system is zero, then its angular momentum remains constant. Mathematically, $\tau_{\text{ext}}=\frac{dL}{dt}$ If no net external torque acts, $\tau_{\text{ext}}=0$ So, $\frac{dL}{dt}=0$ This means angular momentum $L$ does not change with time. Hence, the angular momentum remains constant when net external torque is not applied .

So,

Hence, the angular momentum remains constant when net external torque is not applied.

questions.question_text: Two fly wheels are connected by a non-slipping belt as shown in the figure. $I_{1}=4kgm^{2},r_{1}=20cm$ , $I_{2}=20kgm^{2}$ and $r_{2}=30cm$ . A torque of 10 Nm is applied on the smaller wheel. Then match the entries of column I with appropriate entries of column II. I Quantities II Their numerical Values (in SI units) (a) Angular acceleration of smaller wheel (i) $\frac{5}{3}$ (b) Torque on the larger wheel (ii) $\frac{100}{3}$ (c) Angular acceleration of larger wheel (iii) $\frac{5}{2}$
questions.question_html:
Two fly wheels are connected by a non-slipping belt as shown in the figure. $I_{1}=4kgm^{2},r_{1}=20cm$ , $I_{2}=20kgm^{2}$ and $r_{2}=30cm$ . A torque of 10 Nm is applied on the smaller wheel. Then match the entries of column I with appropriate entries of column II.

I Quantities II Their numerical Values (in SI units)
(a) Angular acceleration of smaller wheel (i) $\frac{5}{3}$
(b) Torque on the larger wheel (ii) $\frac{100}{3}$
(c) Angular acceleration of larger wheel (iii) $\frac{5}{2}$
questions.explanation_text: Explanation The relationship between the torque, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration for each wheel can be established with the following equations: For the smaller wheel: $T_{1}=I_{1}\alpha_{1}$ where $T_{1}$ is the torque applied to the smaller wheel, $I_{1}=4\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ is its moment of inertia, and $\alpha_{1}$ is the angular acceleration. The angular acceleration ratio between the two wheels is given by: $\alpha_{2}r_{2}=\alpha_{1}r_{1}$ where $\alpha_{2}$ is the angular acceleration of the larger wheel, $r_{1}=0.2\text{m}$ , and $r_{2}=0.3\text{m}$ . Given that a torque of 10 Nm is applied to the smaller wheel: $10=\alpha_{1} \times 4$ Solving for $\alpha_{1}$ : $\alpha_{1}=\frac{10}{4}=\frac{5}{2}\text{rad/s}^{2}$ Using the relation for the angular accelerations: $\alpha_{2} \times 0.3=(\frac{5}{2}) \times 0.2$ $\alpha_{2}=\frac{5}{3}\text{rad/s}^{2}$ Finally, for the larger wheel, the torque $T_{2}$ is given by: $T_{2}=I_{2}\alpha_{2}$ where $I_{2}=20\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ . Plugging in the values: $T_{2}=20 \times \frac{5}{3}=\frac{100}{3}\text{Nm}$ Thus, the angular accelerations and the torque can be summarized as follows: Angular acceleration of the smaller wheel $\alpha_{1}=\frac{5}{2}\text{rad/s}^{2}$ Angular acceleration of the larger wheel $\alpha_{2}=\frac{5}{3}\text{rad/s}^{2}$ Torque on the larger wheel $T_{2}=\frac{100}{3}\text{Nm}$
questions.explanation_html:
Explanation

The relationship between the torque, moment of inertia, and angular acceleration for each wheel can be established with the following equations:

For the smaller wheel:

$T_{1}=I_{1}\alpha_{1}$

where $T_{1}$ is the torque applied to the smaller wheel, $I_{1}=4\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ is its moment of inertia, and $\alpha_{1}$ is the angular acceleration.

The angular acceleration ratio between the two wheels is given by:

$\alpha_{2}r_{2}=\alpha_{1}r_{1}$

where $\alpha_{2}$ is the angular acceleration of the larger wheel, $r_{1}=0.2\text{m}$ , and $r_{2}=0.3\text{m}$ .

Given that a torque of 10 Nm is applied to the smaller wheel:

$10=\alpha_{1} \times 4$

Solving for $\alpha_{1}$ :

$\alpha_{1}=\frac{10}{4}=\frac{5}{2}\text{rad/s}^{2}$

Using the relation for the angular accelerations:

$\alpha_{2} \times 0.3=(\frac{5}{2}) \times 0.2$

$\alpha_{2}=\frac{5}{3}\text{rad/s}^{2}$

Finally, for the larger wheel, the torque $T_{2}$ is given by:

$T_{2}=I_{2}\alpha_{2}$

where $I_{2}=20\text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^{2}$ . Plugging in the values:

$T_{2}=20 \times \frac{5}{3}=\frac{100}{3}\text{Nm}$

Thus, the angular accelerations and the torque can be summarized as follows:

Angular acceleration of the smaller wheel $\alpha_{1}=\frac{5}{2}\text{rad/s}^{2}$

Angular acceleration of the larger wheel $\alpha_{2}=\frac{5}{3}\text{rad/s}^{2}$

Torque on the larger wheel $T_{2}=\frac{100}{3}\text{Nm}$

questions.question_text: A body of mass 1 kg is suspended by a weightless string which passes over a frictionless pulley of mass 2 kg as shown in the figure. The mass is released from a height of 1.6 m from the ground. With what velocity does it strike the ground?
questions.question_html: A body of mass 1 kg is suspended by a weightless string which passes over a frictionless pulley of mass 2 kg as shown in the figure. The mass is released from a height of 1.6 m from the ground. With what velocity does it strike the ground?
questions.explanation_text: Given, mass of the body, $m_{1}=1kg$ Mass of pulley, $m_{2}=2kg$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{According to conservation of energy,} \\ & \begin{aligned} m_{1}gℎ & =\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\omega_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{m_{2}R^{2}}{2} \times (\frac{v}{R})^{2} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$ $[ \because I=\frac{m_{2}R^{2}}{2}$ and $\omega=\frac{v}{R}]$ $\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow m_{1}gℎ=\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{4} \times m_{2}v^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow 1 \times 10 \times 1.6=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times v^{2}+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times v^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow v^{2}=4m/s \end{aligned}$

Given, mass of the body, $m_{1}=1kg$

Mass of pulley, $m_{2}=2kg$

$\begin{aligned} & \text{According to conservation of energy,} \\ & \begin{aligned} m_{1}gℎ & =\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2} \\ & =\frac{1}{2}\omega_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{m_{2}R^{2}}{2} \times (\frac{v}{R})^{2} \end{aligned} \end{aligned}$

$[ \because I=\frac{m_{2}R^{2}}{2}$ and $\omega=\frac{v}{R}]$

$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow m_{1}gℎ=\frac{1}{2}m_{1}v^{2}+\frac{1}{4} \times m_{2}v^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow 1 \times 10 \times 1.6=\frac{1}{2} \times 1 \times v^{2}+\frac{1}{4} \times 2 \times v^{2} \\ & \Rightarrow v^{2}=4m/s \end{aligned}$

questions.question_html: The angular speed of a motor wheel is increased from $1200rpm$ to $3120rpm$ in $16s$ . The angular acceleration of the motor wheel is
questions.explanation_text: Given, initial angular frequency of wheel, $f_{0}=1200rpm=\frac{1200}{60}rps=20rps$ $\therefore$ Initial angular velocity, $\omega_{0}=2\pi f_{0}=2\pi \times 20=40\pi rad/s$ Similarly, final angular speed, $\omega=2\pi \times (\frac{3120}{60})rad/s=104\pi rad/s$ $\text{Time,}t=16s$ If $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration of the wheel, then $\begin{aligned} \omega & =\omega_{0}+\alpha t \\ \Rightarrow \alpha & =\frac{\omega-\omega_{0}}{t}=\frac{104\pi-40\pi}{16} \\ & =\frac{64\pi}{16}=4\pi rad/s^{2} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Given, initial angular frequency of wheel,

$f_{0}=1200rpm=\frac{1200}{60}rps=20rps$

$\therefore$ Initial angular velocity,

$\omega_{0}=2\pi f_{0}=2\pi \times 20=40\pi rad/s$

Similarly, final angular speed,

$\omega=2\pi \times (\frac{3120}{60})rad/s=104\pi rad/s$

$\text{Time,}t=16s$

If $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration of the wheel, then

$\begin{aligned} \omega & =\omega_{0}+\alpha t \\ \Rightarrow \alpha & =\frac{\omega-\omega_{0}}{t}=\frac{104\pi-40\pi}{16} \\ & =\frac{64\pi}{16}=4\pi rad/s^{2} \end{aligned}$

(i), we get $\begin{aligned} \frac{3}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}[1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}] \\ \frac{3}{2}-1 & =\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} \\ \frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} & =\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$ Since, for a (a) Sphere, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}$ (b) Ring, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$ (c) Hollow cylinder, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$ (d) Disc, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$ So, the given object is disc.
questions.explanation_html:
As we know, kinetic energy of an object in pure rolling motion is given as

$E=\frac{1}{2}mv_{cm}^{2}(1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}})$

where, $k$ is radius of gyration and $m$ is the mass of the object.

$\Rightarrow \frac{E}{v_{cm}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}[1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}]\text{.... (i)}$

[ $\because$ Given, $m=1kg$ ]

From the given graph, substituting the value of $\frac{E}{v_{cin}^{2}}$ in Eq. (i), we get

$\begin{aligned} \frac{3}{4} & =\frac{1}{2}[1+\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}] \\ \frac{3}{2}-1 & =\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} \\ \frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}} & =\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$

Since, for a

(a) Sphere, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}$

(b) Ring, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$

(c) Hollow cylinder, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=1$

(d) Disc, $\frac{k^{2}}{R^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}$

So, the given object is disc.

questions.question_html: A wheel starting from rest gains an angular velocity of $10rad/s$ after uniformly accelerated for $5s$ . The total angle through which it has turned is

options.label: D

questions.explanation_text: Initial angular velocity of wheel, $\omega_{0}=0$ Final angular velocity, $\omega=10rad/s$ $t=5s$ By first equation of rotational motion, $\begin{aligned} & \omega=\omega_{0}+\alpha t \\ \Rightarrow & 10=0+\alpha \times 5 \\ \Rightarrow & \alpha=\frac{10}{5}=2rad/s^{2} \end{aligned}$ If $\theta$ be the total angle through which wheel has turned, then from, $\begin{aligned} \theta & =\omega_{0}t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2} \\ & =0 \times 5+\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 5^{2}=0+25 \\ \Rightarrow \theta & =25rad \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:
Initial angular velocity of wheel, $\omega_{0}=0$

Final angular velocity, $\omega=10rad/s$

$t=5s$

By first equation of rotational motion,

$\begin{aligned} & \omega=\omega_{0}+\alpha t \\ \Rightarrow & 10=0+\alpha \times 5 \\ \Rightarrow & \alpha=\frac{10}{5}=2rad/s^{2} \end{aligned}$

If $\theta$ be the total angle through which wheel has turned, then from,

$\begin{aligned} \theta & =\omega_{0}t+\frac{1}{2}\alpha t^{2} \\ & =0 \times 5+\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 5^{2}=0+25 \\ \Rightarrow \theta & =25rad \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: The angular momentum of a particle moving uniformly along a straight line about a point $O$ can be analyzed through the concept of cross product $L=r \times p$ , where $L$ is the angular momentum, $r$ is the position vector from the point $O$ to the particle, and $p$ is the linear momentum of the particle. Given the uniform motion along the line from $A$ to $B$ : Since the direction and magnitude of the motion remain constant, As the particle moves from $A$ to $B$ , its distance from point $O$ changes. If the distance between $O$ and the line of motion is constant, then the perpendicular distance from $O$ to the particle's line of motion remains the same, keeping the angular momentum constant. Therefore, the angular momentum of the particle about point $O$ during its motion from $A$ to $B$ remains constant. Option C: remains constant

Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the lamina and passing through the point of intersection of $X$ and $Y$ -axes is
questions.question_html: Moment of inertia of a body about two perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ in the plane of lamina are $20kg-m^{2}$ and $25kg-m^{2}$ , respectively. Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the lamina and passing through the point of intersection of $X$ and $Y$ -axes is
questions.explanation_text: To solve this problem, we use the perpendicular axis theorem. This theorem is applicable to flat, planar objects (laminae) and states that the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane (say the z-axis) is the sum of the moments of inertia about two mutually perpendicular axes (x and y) lying in the plane. Here’s how to apply this theorem: According to the perpendicular axis theorem: $I_{z}=I_{x}+I_{y}$ Substitute the given values: $I_{z}=20\text{kg-m}^{2}+25\text{kg-m}^{2}=45\text{kg-m}^{2}$ Thus, the moment of inertia about the axis perpendicular to the plane is $45\text{kg-m}^{2}.$ The correct answer is Option B.

Here’s how to apply this theorem:

$I_{z}=I_{x}+I_{y}$

Substitute the given values:

$I_{z}=20\text{kg-m}^{2}+25\text{kg-m}^{2}=45\text{kg-m}^{2}$

Thus, the moment of inertia about the axis perpendicular to the plane is $45\text{kg-m}^{2}.$

The correct answer is Option B.
